terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to pack Iain's rucksack and try each method.

tasks.title: Add an item
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `packs.py`, inside the class `Pack`, write a method `add(name, kg)` that puts the item into this pack's `items`: its name as the key and its weight as the value. It refuses a weight that is not above 0 with a `ValueError` whose message names the weight, and an item that would take the pack over its `limit`, with what it holds already, with a `ValueError` whose message names the item and the limit. A pack exactly at its limit is fine. A refused item leaves the pack as it was.

Check makes packs of its own and calls `add` on them, with items that fit, that bring a pack exactly to its limit, that take it over, and weights of 0 and below. It looks at what each pack's `items` holds afterwards, and for a refusal at the kind of error, whether your own raise line raised it and what its message names.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson on a method and on keeping the rule inside.
Write the def line inside the class, lined up with __init__, with self first.
Refuse a weight not above 0, then an item that would take the pack over its limit, each with an if and a raise.
Only after both, put the item into self.items, and try it under the main guard.
hints: Refuse before you change anything: an item already put in the dictionary is still there after a raise.
The pack weighs what all its items weigh added up, and the new item would add `kg` to that. Only more than the limit is refused.

The shape is `def add(self, name, kg):`, then `if kg <= 0:` with a raise, then `if sum(self.items.values()) + kg > self.limit:` with a raise that names `name` and `self.limit`, then `self.items[name] = kg`.

tasks.title: What the pack weighs
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, inside `Pack`, write `weight`, the total of the weights in `items`, as a property: it is read as `pack.weight`, with no round brackets, and worked out from `items` every time it is read, so it is right however `items` changed. The task asks for `@property`. An empty pack weighs 0.

Check makes packs of its own, puts items into their `items` itself, reads `weight` without brackets, puts in one more item and reads it again.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on a value worked out from others.
Write a method that gives back the total of the weights in self.items.
Put @property on the line above its def.
Print iain.weight, without brackets, under the main guard.
hints: A number kept in its own attribute goes wrong the moment items changes without it. Work the total out from items each time.
`@property` on the line above a def lets the method be read like an attribute: `pack.weight`, and Python runs the method for you.
The shape is `@property`, then `def weight(self):` under it, with `return sum(self.items.values())` moved in.

tasks.title: Take an item out
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, inside `Pack`, write a method `remove(name)` that takes the item out of this pack's `items` and gives back its weight. An item that is not in the pack raises `ValueError` from your own raise line, with a message that names it, and leaves the pack as it was.

Check makes packs of its own, puts items into them itself, calls `remove` with items that are in the pack and one that is not, and looks at what it gives back or raises and at what the pack holds afterwards.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on a method and how it changes its object.
Ask first whether the name is in self.items, and raise when it is not.
Keep the item's weight, then take the item out of self.items.
Give the weight back, and try it under the main guard.
hints: Reading a key that is not there stops with a `KeyError`, and the task asks for a `ValueError` of your own that names the item.
A dictionary has a method that takes a key out and gives back its value in one go. Taking the item out of a copy leaves the pack as it was.
The shape is `if name not in self.items:` with `raise ValueError(f"{name} is not in the pack")` under it, then `return self.items.pop(name)`.

tasks.title: A pack without one item
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, inside `Pack`, write a method `without(name)` that gives back a new `Pack` for the same owner and limit, holding every item of this pack but that one. This pack stays as it was, and the two packs do not share their `items`: an item put into one later does not show up in the other.

Check makes packs of its own, calls `without`, and looks at what kind of object comes back, whether it is a new pack, what each pack holds, and whether an item put into the new pack shows up in the old one.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on changing this one or making a new one.
Make a new Pack with this pack's owner and limit.
Put every item but the one named into the new pack's own items.
Give back the new pack, and print both packs' items under the main guard.
hints: `self.items` belongs to this pack. Giving the new pack that same dictionary, or taking the item out of it, changes this pack too.
Calling the class makes a new, empty pack for the owner and limit you give it. Fill its own items from this pack's, leaving one out, or give it a copy and take the item out of the copy.
The shape is `lighter = Pack(self.owner, self.limit)`, then `for item, kg in self.items.items():` with `if item != name:` and `lighter.items[item] = kg`, then `return lighter`.
